We came across this absolutely gorgeous little metallic green Tortoise Beetle on a Solanum plant in the nearby bush. 

Only later when we looked at the piccies did we see there was a tiny winged insect, possibly a wasp or fly (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308080103) having a nap on its back. 

We briefly flipped it over just so you could also see how adorable these little goblins with giant oversized hats really are underneath 😄 

It looks as if this is possibly a Humbug Tortoise Beetle, Conchyloctenia hybrida: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/659090-Conchyloctenia-hybrida and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/659090-Conchyloctenia-hybrida/browse_photos. Thanks for confirming the identification Andrew Schild 🍬

The plant (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308078820) the beetle is sitting on is possibly a Yellow Bitter-Apple, Solanum linnaeanum: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/363523-Solanum-linnaeanum and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/363523-Solanum-linnaeanum/browse_photos.

Edit: Hugh Heron assisted us with further information about this beetle: "This is Conchyloctenia hybrida (“Humbug Tortoise Beetle”): a widespread species throughout Africa including South Africa where its host plants are various Solanum species.  If the identity of Solanum linnaeanum can be confirmed then it is a previously unrecorded host plant.  Larvae are usually found together with adults and derive a measure of protection from the cast skins and filamentous faeces stacked on the “tail fork” as well as the trichomes from the leaf surface (see https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/195827461).  

The small wasp is a parasitoid: possibly one of the Eulophidae.  It is probably waiting for an opportunity to deposit its egg(s) in the papery egg-case that the beetles deposit on the lower leaf surface.  This is an important observation since egg-parasitoids are extremely poorly known for tortoise beetles.  See similar observation and accompanying explanation on https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/110784759. 

The biology of this species has been well studied.  Two references that may be of interest may be found at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263511680 and https://journals.co.za/doi/pdf/10.10520/AJA00128789_3239.

The only other beetle with which this species may be confused on the similar-looking C. tripuncticollis (Three-spot Tortoise Beetle”) that feeds on the same host plants.  It is readily distinguished by the presence of three spots on the pronotum (pronotum is immaculate in C. hybrida): see https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/203999038)." Thanks so much Hugh! 🙂

The first article that Hugh referred to is "Biology of Conchyloctenia hybrida (Coleoptera: Chrysomelidae: Cassidinae) on Solanum campylacanthum subsp. panduriforme" by Tsedal T. Ghebremariam, Kerstin Krüger and Carl Reinhardt in the Annals of the Entomological Society of America 107(4), p. 818-825 (2014): http://dx.doi.org/10.1603/AN13097. It indicates that "Cassidinae are of interest because several neotropical and afrotropical species have been used with considerable success as biological control agents against invasive plant species in different parts of the world, e.g., the United States, Australia, and South Africa. Extensive attack by parasitoids and predators may reduce their success. However, high fertility can counteract mortality owing to natural enemies, resulting in a positive population growth rate." According to the article the green colour in the present beetle apparently indicates sexual maturity 🙂

Interestingly Roberto A. Pantaleoni also remarked, concerning the presence of the winged visitors, that "In Australia, native dung beetles remain attached to the fur of the kangaroos' 'ass' waiting for the production of dung. Kangaroo feces are very dry and should be used immediately, as long as they contain some moisture. 😁 

PS: Of course, a more serious, but more boring, discussion is possible. It concerns the chemical signals coming from the hosts and perceived by the parasitoids, the temporal availability of a resource, and the intra- and inter-specific competition." Thanks for that little glimpse into fascinating things down under Roberto! 😄 

Update: We did a little search and also came across this interesting record from Joggie van Staden where he photographed what may be two parasitising wasps., one next to the Tortoise Beetle, and another also near the elytral split as we found with the fly, here: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1BuPBkZ3o5/. Hugh commented "Joggie van Staden's photo does feature parasitoid wasps.  It is sometimes possible to see parasitoid wasps clambering about oothecae (egg-cases) and laying into the eggs even before the beetle had completed ovipositing." Thanks Hugh!

Thanks Karla Salp tor confirming the ID 🙂

🌍 The flies (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308096465) are possibly Jackal / Freeloader / Filth Flies (Milichiidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=329891&view=species and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/329891-Milichiidae. Thanks for confirming this ID for us Johan Pretorius 🙂 

"Most species are very small and dark. Details of their biology have not yet been properly studied, but they are best known as kleptoparasites of predatory invertebrates"

"Milichiidae are small-to-very-small flies, usually 1 to 3 mm in length. Typically they are black or at least dark."

"The eyes of Milichiidae are often red, though this need not be obvious because many species of the flies are small and dusky. Though the proboscis is fairly long in most species, this is not obvious because it commonly is geniculate, having a knee-like fold in the middle that holds it inconspicuously beneath the head when the animal is not feeding. When it is looking for a place to feed on the prey of a spider or the like, the proboscis is extended, giving an impression of licking...The abdomen is short and broad; it may be impressively distended after a large meal."

"The adults of some species linger close to invertebrate predators, where they act as kleptoparasites, feeding on bodily fluids of the prey."

"The "jackal" habit has been widely documented, with many pictures and references to Millichiidae assembling on the prey of spiders (especially Nephilinae, Oxyopidae, and Thomisidae)...However, a point that is rarely mentioned is that most prey insects do not attract Milichiidae particularly. Instead they seem only to follow the scents exuded by killed prey such as Hemiptera, Heteroptera (stink bugs), and Hymenoptera.This is compatible with the fact that photographs of Milichiidae on prey, almost universally show them on insects that provide such olfactory clues. This would be compatible with the idea that predators that commonly hunt prey that release a dramatic and characteristic olfactory signal, thereby create a niche for suitable kleptoparasites....In general there is suggestive evidence that the kleptoparasitism relies on olfactory clues; for example, some species seem to operate in the dark, and photographs of approaching flies seem to show them flying upwind, which is consistent with scent following."

"Most kleptoparasitic Michiliidae are females, the males presumably having a lower requirement for proteinaceous food; however, as inferred in from the apparent presentation of droplets of food from the proboscises of gorged females, it is possible that the presence of females at the spiders' meals might be reason for males to assemble as well."

"Another activity observed in some species of Milichiidae, shows them to be serving a function analogous to that of cleaner wrasse and cleaner shrimp; they literally scavenge around the chelicerae and anal openings of large spiders, such as species of Araneus and Nephila, that cooperatively spread their wet and sticky chelicerae thus allowing the flies to feed actively all over the bases, fangs and mouth."

Quite some amazing little flies!

Look! 👀 weird little spiny thingies with tall tails! 😃

We were picking a few Swiss Chard* leaves (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308158020) to feed our caterpillars 🐛🐛 when we discovered these exotic fractal-looking larvae underneath!

They seem to wield what might be their excrement on the tips of their tails which they jiggle around! 😄 Quite amazing to watch! 😃 They're each about 5mm long excluding the tail.

It looks as if they may in fact be the larvae of some of the green Shiny Tortoise Beetles, Cassida sp. we previously found in the vicinity before, maybe even those of the Cassida cf. dorsovittata beetles we found mating on the Swiss Chard here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308152302 or of the Cassida cf. viridipennis beetle we found not too far away on some Sweet Potato leaves here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308153586

The larvae of the Cassida sp. reported on INat certainly look quite similar to these larvae: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/126321-Cassida/browse_photos?term_id=1&term_value_id=6, and although there are as yet no piccies of the larvae of Cassida dorsovittata, they do look very similar to those of Cassida viridipennis: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/655675-Cassida-viridipennis/browse_photos?term_id=1&term_value_id=6, and even to those of the predominantly green beetle, Cassida veridis, see for example: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/31288602. As Hugh Heron helpfully pointed out, however, Cassida veridis only occurs in Europe and the Middle East where its host plants are plants of the Lamiaceae. The larvae of the Cassida dorsovittata feed on various members of the Amaranthaceae. Thanks for that additional clarification Hugh! 🙂 

Note: Although we have previously also found some South African Fool's Gold Beetles (Aspidimorpha quadriremis) in the general vicinity here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285587409 and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308157119, the larvae associated with *those* beetles lack the additional centre-line markings which *these* larvae have (compare for example to the South African Fool's Gold Beetle larvae here: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/567886-Aspidimorpha-quadriremis/browse_photos?term_id=1&term_value_id=6)

*The Swiss Chard is Beta vulgaris var. cicla: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/120603-Beta-vulgaris-cicla and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/120603-Beta-vulgaris-cicla/browse_photos.

And there are the munch marks! 😃

We've been coming across quite a few of these beautiful antique gold Tortoise Beetles, Cassidinae subfamily: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=52064&view=species, a Laccoptera sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/336020-Laccoptera and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=336020&view=species.

Possibly Laccoptera cf. ruginosa: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/671746-Laccoptera-ruginosa, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/671746-Laccoptera-ruginosa/browse_photos and similar to one found by Mandy Schubach: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/143146011. 

Hugh Heron informed us that the host plants for Laccoptera ruginosa are members of the Convolvulaceae (the Morning Glories). So far we have mainly been finding them on Sweet Potato plants which are indeed members of that family, but this morning we found two of them located on and near a purple Morning Glory. The Morning Glory leaf is most definitely covered in munch marks! 😄 The other beetle (last piccy) was sitting on a Lantana* leaf - probably for better grip during the rain 😄😅

"Laccoptera is a genus of tortoise beetles in the family Chrysomelidae. There are more than 60 described species in Laccoptera. They are found in Africa, south and east Asia, and Australia."

According to Hugh: "From the photograph, the morning glory looks to be Ipomoea cairica. This is an important host plant for a number of tortoise beetles: from my records, at least nine of our species reproduce on it (ten if we include this observation)." Thanks Hugh! 🙂

That's certainly very interesting! These Morning Glories are certainly absolutely everywhere around here 🙂

We see this one is called the Mile-a-minute Vine, Ipomoea cairica: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/77494-Ipomoea-cairica and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/77494-Ipomoea-cairica/browse_photos. Thanks for confirming the ID for us miaunt 🙂

"Ipomoea cairica is a vining, herbaceous, perennial plant with palmate leaves and large, showy white to lavender flowers. A species of morning glory, it has many common names, including mile-a-minute vine, Messina creeper, Cairo morning glory, coast morning glory and railroad creeper. The species name cairica translates to 'from Cairo', the city where this species was first collected...

The vine blooms occasionally throughout the months, but more profusely from spring to summer.

Its exact native range is uncertain, though it is believed to originate from a rather wide area, ranging from Cape Verde to the Arabian Peninsula, including northern Africa, tropical Africa and the Mediterranean. It covers walls, fences or trees, with stems that can measure more than 10 metres in length. The altitude at which it has been recorded ranges from 250 metres to 2,250 metres.

Because of human dispersal, it occurs today on most continents as an introduced species and is sometimes a noxious weed and an invasive species, such as along the coast of New South Wales...

Some plant nurseries sell this plant as an ornamental plant thanks to its showy purple flowers and as well for its fast growth to quickly cover unsightly fences or walls. It can grow as a separate plant if snapped during attempted removal process. The plant causes respiratory symptoms if ingested.

Ipomoea cairica 'alba', also known as 'white Cairo morning glory', is a variety with white flowers.

Most parts of the plant are edible, such as its leaves, which are eaten when young. And its roots, which can be cooked prior to eating. Zulu people use the plant medicinally, where they make a concoction with its crushed leaves and drink it to heal rashes and fever. The plant in some areas is also considered to have antibiotic properties."

What a fascinating plant! And what a wonderful host to all these precious beetles 🥰🙂

Yaaaay! 😄

We finally managed to get some footage of these extraordinarily peculiar little hairy larvae, not only twitching their little "tails", but *munching* on the Solanum leaves!  😃😄 We really love the way Mark G Wright described the surface-level part of the munching as "mowing the trichomes": https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8408247685939324/?app=fbl

If you look closely (see videos in the Facebook link above), you can see the little feet, head and mouthparts fully engaged in the deliciousness!

These gorgeous hairballs are most likely to be the offspring of some Three Spot Golden Tortoise Beetles, Conchyloctenia cf. tripuncticollis, similar to ones we found here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308149173 and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308146731.

Hugh Heron has formerly commented, regarding these types of larvae which we have previously observed, as follows: "These larvae are those of either Conchyloctenia hybrida or Con. tripuncticollis. Both feed on Solanum plants. Larvae are difficult to distinguish but adults are easy – in Con. tripuncticollis there are three black spots on the pronotum (none for Con. hybrida). Both species occur in the Eastern Cape so it may be necessary to raise a larva to adulthood to make an identification." 

We have indeed previously also seen a single Humbug Tortoise Beetle, Conchyloctenia hybrida: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/659090-Conchyloctenia-hybrida and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/659090-Conchyloctenia-hybrida/browse_photos, in the bush: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308077910, so this may also be a possibility. We see some piccies of the larvae listed on iNat here: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/659090-Conchyloctenia-hybrida/browse_photos. They do, however, appear to be *darker beige* in colour, rather than *pale* like these ones, and the lateral spines are not all as predominantly *black* as appears to be the case here 🤔

We did also only see one of these beetles as compared to dozens of Three Spot Golden Tortoise Beetles, so it's numerically more likely to be one of the larvae of the formerly-mentioned beetles, but it certainly remains a possibility...

We recently found these interesting larvae...on our Sweet Potato 🍠 plants.

We've certainly seen some fascinating hairy-tailed Tortoise Beetle larvae so far:

A. We saw some in the nearby bush on Solanum plants here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308146731 and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308149173 which may possibly either be the larvae of some Three Spot Golden Tortoise Beetles, Conchyloctenia cf. tripuncticollis or those of some Humbug Tortoise Beetles, Conchyloctenia cf. hybrida.

B. We saw some others on some Swiss Chard in the garden here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308155480 which look similar to the larvae of some green Shiny Tortoise Beetles, Cassida sp., which may possibly be the larvae of either some Cassida cf. dorsovittata, or some Cassida cf. viridipennis Tortoise Beetles.

The different types of larvae on these Sweet Potato leaves, however, do not look the same as any of these types that we have previously encountered...🤔

🌍 As for the...paler greenish larvae - the potential parent Tortoise Beetles we have thus far found in the garden include the following:

1) Gorgeous golden South African Fool's Gold Beetles, Aspidimorpha quadriremis, here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285587409, here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308157119, and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285589878.

2) A slightly more unusual-looking turquoise and gold Tortoise Beetle: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308490647, which we initially thought was possibly similar to Aspidimorpha cf. icterica, but which apparently is actually another South African Fool's Gold Beetle,

3) A golden lined Tortoise Beetle possibly similar to Aspidimorpha cf. areata:  https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308178220

4) Some beautiful antique gold Tortoise Beetles, possibly similar to Laccoptera cf. ruginosa:  https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308102332 and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/308129656 and

Another group at Encontro das Águas State Park. We watched a member of this group catch a large catfish. Subsequently, there was an altercation over the fish, one individual grabbing at least part of it from the one that caught it--fifth image here.
The sixth image shows the "thief" quite close to the boat. We did not chase, lure them in, or feed them--they seemed to enjoy being near the boats. 
Prey is perhaps a Jaú Catfish (Zungaro species, Pimelodidae).

Giant Otter, Ariranha - Pteronura brasiliensis
It was a real treat to see these, as I had not realized they were found outside of the Amazon Basin. Though globally endangered, they seem to be doing well in Encontro das Águas State Park and showed no fear of the tourist-laden boats. This one was spotted bathing and splashing across the river channel, swam over to investigate us, then caught an eel and consumed it noisily. 

The eel is likely a Marbled Swamp Eel (Synbranchus marmoratus), or a relative.

Fascinating...

On 16 July we discovered these rather peculiar-looking larvae on a plant (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/309463126) in the park. 

From some previous discussions with Suncana Bradley we knew that these aren't caterpillars, but more likely Sawfly larvae.

Intrigued we collected a few for rearing along with a few cuttings from the plant...

Unfortunately the cuttings were rather woody and kept wilting even though put them in water, so we kept returning to gather more cuttings until we became concerned that we'd be pruning the plant too far and on 20 July we rather returned the larvae to what was left of the bush 😊

While we were doing so we spotted a really laaarge larva (just over 25mm long) that looked as if it might nearly be ready to pupate, so we collected it along with another small cutting and placed it into a container.

We had read that Sawflies tend to drop to the soil in order to pupate, so we filled the bottom of the container with soil.

The chubby little larva munched and munched as you can see in the second and third videos (see Facebook link above) and on 25 July it dropped to the bottom of the container to pupate in the soil.

We found that quite amazing, so after another two days we carefully dug it up to see what it looks like and then returned it back into the soil.

The wait was on...what, if anything, would come out of that beautiful little cocoon we wondered? 🤔  

Edit1: According to Simon van Noort the plant is possibly a member of the Camphorbushes, Tarchonanthus sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/474040-Tarchonanthus and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=474040&view=species. That's very helpful, thanks Simon! 🙂 

Update: After a tense month of misting the soil and watching what would happen, we're very happy to announce the arrival of a very special little one 🧡🖤🤗: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/309649273.

It looks as if it's possibly an Arge whiteheadi: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/1631502-Arge-whiteheadi and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/1631502-Arge-whiteheadi/browse_photos.

Edit2: We subsequently sent messages to both Andreas Taeger and Simon van Noort telling them the good news about the arrival of the little one.

Andreas replied that: "It's interesting to see this successful rearing, even if the host plant is not safely identified.

The photos of the female leave for me no doubt that this is A. whiteheadi. It seems to me rather unlikely that there is "doppelganger"."

So this little one is evidently also a little lady - thanks so much Andreas! 🙂

Simon and Martin Hauser also helpfully confirmed the ID. Thanks Simon and Martin! 🙂

Northern Grass Mantis, Brunner's Mantis, Brunner's stick mantis - Brunneria borealis (female--parthenogenetic species, larger one ~80 mm) One of the survey leaders spotted these two stick mantids struggling. The smaller one was soon decapitated (image 2) and consumed. We thought this was a male being killed in a mating attempt, but another of the zoologists mentioned this species is parthenogenetic, comprised only of females. This must have been a larger female attacking a smaller one. A first for me, and the species is fascinating. The North American species is all female. The other species are South American and contain both males and females. I believe all species are flightless. They are mostly restricted to grasslands where found. One idea is that the North American species came from dispersal of South American ancestors when grasslands were more widespread in the Pliocene, 2.6-5.3 million years ago (Rehn, 1958). I don't know if more modern research has confirmed this. Also posted at: https://bugguide.net/node/view/2490359 References - BugGuide bugguide.net/node/view/34147 - Rehn (1958). I don't have the resources to investigate this very far, it would need a powerful microscope, a medium for growing fungal cultures etc.) I might try taste but I'm a bit reluctant to risk that if ergot is involved. "Rubus idaeus (raspberry, also called red raspberry or occasionally European red raspberry to distinguish it from other raspberry species) is a red-fruited species of Rubus native to Europe and northern Asia and commonly cultivated in other temperate regions...

Plants of Rubus idaeus are generally perennials, which bear biennial stems ("canes") from a perennial root system. In its first year, a new, unbranched stem ("primocane") grows vigorously to its full height of 1.5–2.5 m, bearing large pinnately compound leaves with five or seven leaflets, but usually no flowers. In its second year (as a "floricane"), a stem does not grow taller, but produces several side shoots, which bear smaller leaves with three or five leaflets. The flowers are produced in late spring on short racemes on the tips of these side shoots, each flower about 1 cm diameter with five white petals. The fruit is red, edible, and sweet but tart-flavoured, produced in summer or early autumn; in botanical terminology, it is not a berry at all, but an aggregate fruit of numerous drupelets around a central core. In raspberries (various species of Rubus subgenus Idaeobatus), the drupelets separate from the core when picked, leaving a hollow fruit, whereas in blackberries and most other species of Rubus, the drupelets stay attached to the core.

Its fruit persists for an average of 12 days, and bears an average of 35.2 seeds per fruit. Wild fruits average 76.3% water, and their dry weight includes 39.6% carbohydrates and 2.2% lipids.

As a wild plant, R. idaeus typically grows in forests, forming open stands under a tree canopy, and denser stands in clearings. In the south of its range (southern Europe and central Asia), it occurs only at high altitudes in mountains. The species name idaeus refers to its occurrence on Mount Ida near Troy in what is now northwest Turkey, where the ancient Greeks were most familiar with it.

R. idaeus is grown primarily for its fruits, but occasionally for its leaves, roots, or other parts.

The fruit of R. idaeus is an important food crop, though most modern commercial raspberry cultivars derive from hybrids between R. idaeus and R. strigosus. The fruits of wild plants have a sweet taste and are very aromatic."

See Part II here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316049504.

09 September (piccies 1-3): We recently collected this little larva in the hopes of seeing what it would become. 

We put the branch we found it on, together with a few extra branches, into some water.

The plant (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316231176) is a Coast (or Coastal) Silver-Oak, Brachylaena discolor: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/567699-Brachylaena-discolor and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/567699-Brachylaena-discolor/browse_photos

The larva is quite honey-coloured, has several white markings on top, several oval shapes on the region covering the head, spines all around and two long "horns" at the rear. The little feet are surprisingly well hidden underneath, and it seems to be rather sedentary. 🤗

10 September around 9:00 (piccies 4-9): The larva with beautifully artistic munch marks on top of one of the leaves - we don't see it actually eating, but there's plenty of evidence that it clearly does! 😄 It looks as if it's about 9mm long excluding the "horns" at the back.

10 September around 15:30 (piccy 10): The larva is changing colour and looks paler. It has moved to another old leaf. 

11 September (piccies 11-15): The larva is surprisingly mobile and somehow seems to get around to other leaves (when we're not looking! 🤭).

Edit: Hugh Heron subsequently assisted us with identifying the larva and the adult that later emerged as documented in Part IV of this post: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316219415.

"Larva ultimately yielded Basipta glauca – see comment at https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316223866. The colouring and markings on the final-instar larva are different to those of Basipta stolida … compare with https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/152817404 and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/66705546." 

Thanks so much Hugh - what a fascinating journey! 🙂

https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/652645-Basipta-glauca and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/652645-Basipta-glauca/browse_photos. Thanks Rob Westerduijn for confirming the ID for us 🙂

"Musca autumnalis, the face fly or autumn housefly, is a pest of cattle and horses.

The face fly is similar to the closely related housefly but is slightly larger, averaging about 7–8 mm long and grey in colour with four dark stripes on the thorax, with a grey-black patterned abdomen. Like many true flies, in the males, the eyes almost touch when viewed from above...

Adult face flies will emerge from winter hibernation [in spring]. During the daytime, they feed on manure juices and plant sugars. On cattle and horses, they feed on secretions around the eyes, mouth and nostrils. The adult flies will also feed on the hosts' blood through wounds such as horse-fly bites. A larger proportion of face flies on the host will be females, as they have a higher need for protein provided by animal hosts. At night, both sexes will rest on vegetation.

Females deposit eggs on fresh cow manure and these hatch within hours after deposition. The yellowish-white maggots feed on the microbial flora and fauna of the manure and pass through three larval stages (instars), growing to about 12 mm long, then developing into white pupae. They emerge as adults about 10 to 20 days after egg deposition, depending on the temperature.

M. autumnalis is considered a pest species, as it transmits the eyeworm Thelazia rhodesi to cattle and horses, and pinkeye (infectious bovine keratoconjunctivitis) to cattle."

**A sweet little Sweet Potato larva Part Ia of Ic**
See Part Ib here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316912663.

On 14 September we found this little larva on some Sweet Potato 🍠 vines (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316960800) with Tortoise Beetle oothecae that we had brought in from the garden for rearing.

It's really cute and wiggly-looking, with tiny spines all along the edge and tiny feet underneath..

This is the bit of footage we managed to take of it while we could (also see Part Ib: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316912663) - we were really excited to see it. 🙂

The next day we couldn't find it anywhere, and on 16 September all we could find was a Jumping Spider 😬 and this dark mark on a leaf (see Part Ic: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316913294) which we hadn't noticed before...the white thing next to it is probably a white mite of some sort...

We removed the Spidey and thought it might sadly have eaten the larva because we couldn't really see any life at the dark mark on the leaf...😥

Then some days later, on 22 September, still thinking of the sweet little larva, we re-searched the entire branch and its leaves to see if the little larva hadn't maybe, just maybe wondered off somewhere 🤞, but no...all we could find again was the dark mark on the leaf...

We decided to take a closer look at it, even having a closer look underneath...we realised it's rather a similar size to the length of the larva that we measured...hmmmmm...🔍🤔😄 

Well what else can you do but wait and hope? 😊 

Update: Guess what happened on the evening of  26 September? 🤎🤭 Have a little look here  👀: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316950258. Thanks Nikie Scott for confirming the ID of this little larva for us 🙂 Interestingly, according to Nikie, there is: "Lots of information with photographs of both the larvae and adults on page 60 of Dr Visser's Vegetable Pest book (2011)." Thanks Nikie! 🙂

**A sweet little Sweet Potato larva Part IIa of IIe**
See Part IIb here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316951272

See Part I here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316912325

On 14 September we found a yellowish spiny larva on some Sweet Potato 🍠 vines: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316912325.

It subsequently disappeared, and we feared that it had been eaten by a little Jumping Spider 😬 Then we noticed a peculiar dark mark on a nearby leaf...we realised that it was similar in size to the length of the larva...hmmmmm...🔍🤔 What else could we do but wait and hope? 😊 

Well, at around 21:15 last night, on 26 September, we discovered that this little Beetle must *just* have emerged from the one end of the brown pocket! 🤎😃

We were sooooo glad to see that the "larva" was still alive! 😅🥰🤗

Here it is, munching next to the tiny brown sleeping bag it must have made for itself by tunneling between the leaf layers from underneath - how incredibly innovative! 

Although it was quite dark, we managed to get some footage of it eating and walking around, and we even managed to film it from underneath as it walked on some glass 🤭 (see videos in the Facebook link above or Parts IIa-d by following the links above).

When we first saw the beetle, we remembered that we had recently, on 15 September, seen a rather similar "knobblechoc-looking" beetle, also about 4mm long, on our Lemon 🍋 tree: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/315200857.

This little Beetle is then possibly also an Oncocephala sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/347770-Oncocephala and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=347770.

It looks similar to Oncocephala cf. promontorii: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/347776-Oncocephala-promontorii and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/347776-Oncocephala-promontorii/browse_photos.

This morning, when it was light, we took a few more piccies (see Part IIe here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316953490)

With better lighting the brown colouring and knobblechoc protrusions on the back are more visible. 🍫🤎🤗 How completely adorable!

Edit: Riaan Stals subsequently pointed us to a rather excellent article all about this little wonder by Chaboo CS, Grobbelaar E, Heron HDC (2010) An African leaf miner, Oncocephala promontorii Péringuey, 1898 (Chrysomelidae: Cassidinae: Oncocephalini): biological notes and host records. Coleopterists Bulletin 64(1): 21–29. doi:10.1649/0010-065X-64.1.21. here: https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Elizabeth-Grobbelaar/publication/216682241_An_African_Leaf_Miner_Oncocephala_promontorii_Peringuey_1898_Chrysomelidae_Cassidinae_Oncocephalini_Biological_Notes_and_Host_Records. There's a real wealth of fascinating facts and observations about this little creature in this article! Thanks so much Riaan! 🙂 

"Habitats, host plants, and preliminary biological notes are documented for Oncocephala promontorii Peringuey, 1898 for the first time. The beetle occurs in open areas of coastal grassland, forest margin, and disturbed urban areas where their Convolvulaceae host plants are found. Seven host plants are verified for the species in the field Convolvulus arvensis L., Convolvulus farinosus L., Ipomoea batatas (L.) Lam., Ipomoea ficifolia Lindl., Ipomoea obscura (L.) Ker Gawl., Ipomoea wightii (Wall.) Choisy, and an unidentified Ipomoea sp. Ipomoea purpurea (L.) Roth is recorded as a host from museum specimen labels. Two additional plants, Ipomoea cairica (L.) Sweet and Ipomoea coccinea L., showed feeding traces that we attribute to O. promontorii. The larvae are solitary miners that produce curvilinear to vermiform mines in the host plant leaves. Pupation is solitary in a separate pupal chamber/mine in the leaf. Imagines are generally solitary, exposed folivores that produce narrow linear feeding trenches in the dorsal leaf surface. Copulation is commonly observed on the dorsal leaf surface."

These Sweet Potato 🍠 vines (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316963028) truly are an endless source of *the* most fascinating forms of life!

A little while ago, after a few rainy days, we discovered this enormous explosion of bugs...

They look very much like the bugs we also later found here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/317757061.

Unlike *that* rather jolly cluster of bugs however, it seems this cluster is significantly larger and they seem to be fighting with one another! ☹

Most surprisingly we discovered one bug apparently feeding on a deceased bug and a third bug trying to do the same with the feeding bug!

These are possibly Milkweed Bugs, Oncopeltus famelicus: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/577832-Oncopeltus-famelicus and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/577832-Oncopeltus-famelicus/browse_photos. Thanks Dawid Jacobs for confirming the ID for us 🙂

From what we could find on this topic, cannibalism has apparently been observed under extreme conditions in another species of the same genus, Oncopeltus faciatius here: https://bugguide.net/node/view/1582421 and here: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28308908/ "Penetration of the cuticle seems to be effected mainly by mechanical forces. No chitin-splitting enzyme could be detected in the saliva."

Perhaps it was a case of too much rain and too many bugs clustering together causing them to become agitated with one another...

Edit: Tony Rebelo also gave some suggestions about this topic (https://www.inaturalist.org/posts/115753-q-a#activity_comment_8cbdd4d8-bb46-43f5-b543-8bf637ba8844): "Cannibalization of broodmates is fairly common with abundant-poor resource dynamics. We find it in birds of prey, tadpoles and many invertebrates.

see https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000334722500123X
for birds: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siblicide" Thanks so much Tony! 🙂

Cory Chiappone pointed out that the aphids in this post are "Not bright enough yellow for Oleander Aphid Aphis nerii". We asked Natalie Hernandez, mentioning that we believe the plant to be Canary Creeper, Senecio tamoides, and she commented that: "These are definitely not Aphis nerii. In addition to being the wrong color, their legs and antennae are mostly pale. Aphis nerii usually have mostly black appendages.

Possibly Aphis spiraecola, but there are a number of Aphis known to colonize senecio and I cannot zoom in enough to confirm species."

She also provided a number of very interesting links:

https://aphidsonworldsplants.info/C_HOSTS_Sap_Sen/#Senecio: A list of all aphids that feed on Senecio sp. plants
https://influentialpoints.com/Gallery/Aphis_nerii_oleander_aphid.htm: A description of the Milkweed Aphid
https://influentialpoints.com/Gallery/Aphis_spiraecola_spirea_aphid.htm: A description of Aphis spiraecola

She also mentioned that "Aphis is the largest genus in the family with over 500 described species."

The link https://influentialpoints.com/Gallery/Aphis_aphids.htm contains a very nice description of this genus:

"Aphis are very small to rather large aphids with a body that is broadly oval in shape and never very elongate. The dorsal body cuticle is membranous with a variable amount of dark sclerotic markings. Marginal tubercles are almost always present on the pronotum and on some of the abdominal segments. The siphunculi are more or less cylindrical or tapering, never distinctly swollen. The cauda is finger shaped, tongue shaped or bluntly subtriangular. The legs are variably pigmented, but rarely entirely dark.

There are about 500 species in the Aphis genus. Most species...have a sexual stage in the life cycle and pass the winter in the egg stage. Others reproduce parthenogenetically all year round especially in warmer climates. Aphis species feed on a great variety of different plants, but never on sedges (Cyperaceae) and very rarely on grasses (Poaceae). Some species alternate hosts seasonally between a woody primary host and a herbaceous summer host. But many species do not host alternate, instead spending the complete life cycle on one species of plant. Aphis species are frequently ant attended and many are important crop pests."

There's another description here: https://aphidsonworldsplants.info/d_APHIDS_A/#Aphis:

"The largest aphid genus containing more than 500 species, most of which occur in the northern hemisphere, but a few are native to South America, New Zealand, and Australia.  Mostly they are small to medium‑sized aphids, often greenish but varying from pale to dark green, and sometimes yellow, brown, reddish, or black.  Most species live on shrubs or herbs, with relatively few on trees.  They usually live on the young foliage and often distort the leaves, but some species live on young twigs or at the base of the stem, or on the roots.  Most species are attended by ants which may construct earthen shelters for the species living just above soil level."

Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1MWnGjwVmm **Part Ia of Ic: How amazingly weird is *this*??!** 😃 See Part Ib here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/319735972. On 14 September we discovered a little larva on some Sweet Potato vines: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316912325. After a while it disappeared and we had no idea where it went! 🤔 At around that time, we also happened to noticed a tiny brown patch on one of the leaves, so we wondered if it hadn't possibly tunneled into the leaf in order to pupate there? 🤔 Much to our delight, on the evening of 26 September, we discovered that a strange little knobble-chock-looking beetle had emerged from what must then definitely have been its pupation "sleeping bag": https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/316950258. 🤎😃 The larva must indeed have tunneled in from the back of the leaf, and pupated from the brown "sleeping bag" mound that was visible on the upper side of the leaf. We subsequently learned that it was apparently a Hispine Beetle, an Oncocephala sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/347770-Oncocephala and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=347770. More specifically it was an Oncocephala cf. promontorii: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/347776-Oncocephala-promontorii and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/347776-Oncocephala-promontorii/browse_photos. So back to *these* peculiar little beetles...👀🤔 They emerged from some Sweet Potato vines (separately posted here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/319784518) from our garden.
Top left and right - the pupa collected on 26 September and the emerging beetle (around 08:00 on 07 October) Bottom left and right - the pupa collected on 25 September and the emerging beetle (around 08:20 on 07 October) They appear to be rather pale, not brownish-black!
The first pupa - the larva is in the "sleeping bag" 🤭 We collected this leaf on 26 September.

It must have emerged from the little pupal "sleeping bag" on a leaf that we collected on 26 September. Here we see some darker markings on the pronotum...
The "knobbles" on the back are clearly there! 😃
The view from underneath through a piece of glass - too cute! 🤭
About 20 minutes later, at around 08:20, we discovered a second beetle (second set of piccies in the Facebook link above or see Part Ic of this post: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/319736295). The second beetle is just as pale as the first...
It must have emerged from the little pupal "sleeping bag" on a leaf we collected on 26 September. 🌍 According to "Diversity of spider families parasitized by fungal pathogens: a global review" by  Martin Nyffeler and Nigel Hywel-Jones in The Journal of Arachnology, 52(2):151-185 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1636/JoA-S-23-007 "Salticids [Jumping Spiders] were the dominant fungus-infected above-ground spiders of the Tropics/Subtropics...

The predominance of the salticids among the fungus-infected spiders may be explained by the fact that salticids: (i) are among the most common spiders in warmer areas, thus, making available a huge number of potential hosts for fungal attacks; and (ii) that these spiders are highly exposed to the attacks by airborne fungal spores while searching plant surfaces for prey or potential mates during daylight hours."

According to the article, "Cordycipitaceae was the most prominent spider-pathogenic fungal family, accounting for ca. three-quarters of all recorded spider infections. Within the Cordycipitaceae, the genus Gibellula (including its sexual morph Torrubiella) is a particularly species-rich and widespread group of specific spider-pathogenic fungi."

It looks as if our little spider was infected by a Gibellula sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/328134-Gibellula and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/328134-Gibellula/browse_photos.

Meet "Thorn" 🤭🤗

On 09 September we collected some branches with Tortoise Beetle oothecae in the hopes of rearing them...

On 16 September, an entire week later, we suddenly noticed *this* moving around! 😃

What a surprise! 😃 

Apparently this little thing had been there all along, but we didn't see it! 

It looks just like a walking thorn, only much more ornately decorated and gentle, but we decided to name it "Thorn"! 🤭 

Thorn is a Bagworm, a member of the Bagworm Moths (Psychidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/61415-Psychidae and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=61415&view=species. Thanks só much Johan Pretorius for always helping us with all these IDs! 🙂

https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/567699-Brachylaena-discolor and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/567699-Brachylaena-discolor/browse_photos.

We tried to establish what Thorn likes to eat, so we returned to the tree and collected a few different samples, including Silver-Oak bark and lichen...

We offered them to Thorn, who only briefly nibbled on a piece of freshly sliced bark, so we rather reluctantly returned Thorn to the tree - goodbye Thorn - we're going to miss you ! 😥😘

What a gorgeous creature, and what a privilege to have spent some time together 🥰🤗

Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps, sawflies) are characterized by two pairs of membranous wings joined by tiny hooks (hamuli), chewing or chewing-sucking mouthparts, complete metamorphosis, and mandibulate mouthparts. Hymenoptera are predators. Hymenoptera order is split into sawflies (broad waist) and wasps/bees/ants (narrow waist).

Key Characteristics of Hymenoptera:

• Diversity: Over 150,000 described species worldwide, including ants, bees, wasps, and sawflies.
• Wings: Typically two pairs of membranous wings; forewings larger than hindwings. The wings are coupled by hamuli (small hooks). Some castes (e.g., worker ants) are wingless.
• Body Form:• In Symphyta (sawflies, horntails): broad connection between thorax and abdomen.
• In Apocrita (ants, bees, wasps): narrow “wasp waist” between thorax and abdomen.

• Mouthparts: Primarily mandibulate (chewing); in bees, modified into a chewing-lapping apparatus for nectar.
• Metamorphosis: Holometabolous (complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult).
• Feeding:• Sawfly larvae are herbivorous.
• Many wasps are predatory or parasitoid, laying eggs in or on other insects.
• Bees are nectar and pollen feeders, crucial pollinators.
• Ants are omnivorous, with diverse diets.

• Sociality: Includes some of the most advanced eusocial insects (ants, honeybees, some wasps), with division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlapping generations. Most species, however, are solitary.
• Ecological Role:• Pollinators (bees, some wasps).
• Biological control agents (parasitoid wasps regulating pest populations).
• Soil engineers and ecosystem influencers (ants).

The Amargosa River stretches about 185 miles (298 km), winding through southern Nevada into eastern California before vanishing into Death Valley’s Badwater Basin. It rises near Pahute Mesa in Nye County and drains a vast desert basin of roughly 14,000 square kilometers. For most of its course the river flows underground, hidden within aquifers, surfacing only in rare segments near Beatty, Nevada, and in California’s Amargosa Canyon near Tecopa. These brief above-ground stretches sustain pockets of dense vegetation and wildlife, contrasting sharply with the arid desert surroundings. The river’s intermittent surface flow is often triggered by storms, but its subterranean path is continuous, feeding ecosystems quietly beneath the desert floor. Its protected 26-mile scenic corridor between Shoshone and Dumont Dunes highlights both its ecological importance and its unusual character as a river that is at once extensive in reach yet elusive in visibility.

Amargosa River is "often called the "Crown Jewel of the Mojave Desert." The Amargosa River is the only free-flowing river in the Death Valley region of the Mojave Desert, providing a rare and lush riparian habitat in the desert" . . . Dancers (Argia genus): "is a diverse genus which contains about 114 species and many more to be described. It is also the largest genus in Argiinae. They are found in the Western Hemisphere. This genus of Damselflies are known as Dancers because of the distinctive jerky form of flight they use which contrasts with the straightforward direct flight of bluets, forktails and other pond damselflies. They are usually to be seen in the open where they catch flying insects on the wing rather than flying about among vegetation picking off sedentary prey items. They tend to land and perch flat on the ground, logs and rocks.[2] When perched, they usually hold their wing slightly raised above the abdomen. The males of most species are some combination of black and blue but they can easily be told from similarly coloured bluets by their mode of flight. Some species have red eyes and others a copper-coloured thorax. Many species have humeral stripes, either notched or forked at the end or narrowed in the centre. The wings have short petioles and are relatively broad close to the base. Unlike most of the Coenagrionidae, dancers are often associated with flowing water." https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/47977-Argia

Dragonflies and Damselflies are flying insects in the Order Odonata. Adults are highly aerial. Larvae are aquatic and predatory. Adult dragonflies are characterized by a pair of large, multifaceted compound eyes, two pairs of strong, transparent wings, sometimes with colored patches, and an elongated body. Dragonflies can be mistaken for the closely related Damselflies, but the wings of most dragonflies are held flat, outward at a right angle, away from the body, while damselflies hold their wings folded at rest, above, or parallel to the abdomen. Dragonflies are agile fliers, while damselflies have a weaker, fluttery flight.
Odonata pairs oviposit in tandem. They are joined together while laying eggs on water. When joined together, they exhibit "mate-guarding" behavior while the female lays eggs with tail-dipping motions into water. They stay fairly low between descents and often tap the water repeatedly before moving a short distance and doing it again.

description:
Watching my shopping center Hooded Mergansers for a while, I got to see an interesting sequence of behavior. They would loaf for a while near center of the pond and then go to edge and dive repeatedly, apparently feeding. Just as I was wondering what they were after, the female emerged with a thrashing crayfish and struggled with it for five minutes or so. It appeared to be attempting to remove the pincers. Eventually the crayfish, shorn of pincers, was swallowed and the mergansers returned to the center of the pond for a rest. 
Edit. I believe the prey is the Red Swamp Crayfish, *Procambarus clarkii*. This is an invasive species in North Carolina, so good to see it being consumed by native waterfowl.

Note. The "North Carolina, US critically imperiled (S1B,S4N)by NatureServe" annotation needs to be updated. Breeding has become common in much of the state, including the Piedmont. This increase is likely due to the increase in beaver ponds with standing dead trees. Beavers, extirpated in the state by 1897, have become common in after reintroductions starting in the 1930's (https://www.ncwildlife.gov/media/1929/open). 
Hooded Mergansers have long been common in the state during the winter.

Redhead - Aythya americana (male, feeding on fish)
Location: Durham NC (USA)
I've been birding at this lake for over 20 years, and I have seldom seen Redheads here. Cold weather for several weeks this winter has apparently brought in good numbers.
Redheads dabbled and dove for vegetation in the shallows, but they also caught fish, which they fought over. In addition, they tried to steal fish from Hooded Mergansers. 
References I find on waterfowl do not mention fish as a food item for Redhead. They normally feed on aquatic vegetation and aquatic invertebrates. An astute friend suggested the fish were paralyzed, or killed, by the cold weather. Aha!

With Don Fraser; a visit to see how many butterflies and other insects we could find.

Our itinerary for today was:

0924-1122: Rattlesnake Camp Road thistle pond. The weather at the start was sunny and 76 degrees ("feels like" 76), with a light breeze. I counted the following butterflies, mostly on the blooming Bristle Thistles: 68 swallowtails, 69 skippers, 7 sulphurs, and 1 Gulf Fritillary. This was the day that I learned that Larger Florida Mantises are fucking killing machines, something I had wondered about in 2023, as the numbers of skippers declined through the fall season. Don and I watched one mantis capture and consume one Twin-spot Skipper (1024-1035), then quickly capture and consume a second Twin-spot Skipper (1037-1041), then capture and consume a third Twin-spot Skipper (1055-1108), then instantly start hunting a Palmetto Skipper, which escaped at the last possible milli-second, and then try to capture a Palamedes Swallowtail, which also escaped at the last milli-second. I did not enjoy watching the killing sequences, but I did not intervene at all.
 
1204-1226: Scrub Island Road, west end turnaround.

1239-1307: 3 Bridge Road. Dukes' Skipper spot

1313-1325: 3 Bridge Road, Buford Spring parking lot.

1336-1429: Indigo Lane sandhills.

We left the WEA around 1445.
